1_sample_cost: The policy was trained on the 150,000 samples so instead of deriving the kinematics or tuning a state machine,
it was learned by trial and error. Both controllers had 100% success, but this task did not require solution derivation
which might be more convenient depending on the need.
2_where_knowledge_lives: The Jacobian, the damped least-squares update, and the state machine is easier to inspect
because the output directly points to the input. For example, the saturated gain failure pointed to the joint value
that caused it. Whereas, the reward and the network weights are distributed so you cannot see the input that caused the
failure just that it failed at the specific input variable.
3_model_matters_to_both: In section 1, defect 3 the unlimited and undamped drawer slide joint would have broken the classical controller.
Defect 4 would have corrupted the RL without crashing the training.
The  training would still run and the policy would still learn to succeed but the physics would be unrealistic.
4_failure_modes: Learned policy specific: if a policy is trained under domain randomization distribution it can fail when outside
that distribution with no warning whereas a controller would fail to converge visibly. Controller specific: Hand
selecting constants that are wrong for the system. The saturated gain failure that I saw came from a fixed gain
damping pair which could be wrong for the configuration.
5_recommendation: For this drawer I would ship the classical controller since it was able to pass and complete the task.
However, if the dynamics became more complicated that a kinematic model was difficult to derive then
it would make more sense to switch to RL.
